You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Lion

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching the lion is most commonly a symbol of royal, sovereign power and majesty, applied above all to Jesus Christ as the 'Lion of the tribe of Judah'—the conquering messianic King descended from Judah and David. The image conveys kingship, strength, courage, and victorious authority.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Revelation 5:5 (Christ as 'the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David' who has conquered)",
    "Genesis 49:9-10 (Jacob's blessing: 'Judah is a lion's cub... the scepter shall not depart from Judah')",

    "Numbers 23:24; 24:9 (Israel rising up like a lion in Balaam's oracles)"
  ],

      "basis": [
        "1 Peter 5:8",
        "Psalm 22:13, 21 (lions surrounding and menacing the righteous sufferer, read Christologically of the passion)",
        "2 Timothy 4:17 ('rescued from the lion's mouth')"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {

        "Amos 1:2; 3:8 ('The lion has roared; who will not fear?')",
        "Jeremiah 25:38; 49:19",
        "Lamentations 3:10",
        "Isaiah 31:4"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Hostile earthly kingdoms, kings, or oppressive enemies of God's people (e.g., Babylon; Nebuchadnezzar's lion-beast in Daniel's vision; wicked rulers).",
      "basis": [

      "prominence": "common"

      "meaning": "In the traditional four-living-creatures scheme, the lion as the emblem of Mark the Evangelist (patristic and iconographic tradition following Irenaeus, Jerome, and Augustine, with varying assignments).",

      "prominence": "minority"

    {
      "meaning": "Deliverance/vindication motif: God shutting the lions' mouths as a type of rescue of the faithful and, in some patristic readings, a type of Christ's resurrection from the pit.",

        "Daniel 6:16-23",
        "Hebrews 11:33",
        "Psalm 91:13"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"

  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "The lion is a well-recognized but deliberately bivalent biblical symbol: interpreters across traditions (patristic, medieval bestiary, Reformation, and modern evangelical/academic) uniformly note that context determines whether it signifies Christ/God in regal power or Satan/enemies in devouring menace. The Christological 'Lion of Judah' reading is the most frequently cited primary meaning in Christian teaching (reinforced culturally by C.S. Lewis's Aslan), with 1 Peter 5:8's satanic lion as the standard counterpoint. Because the symbol is context-dependent rather than univocal, the consensus is on this dual/polyvalent framework rather than on a single fixed referent."
}

      "basis": [

        "Traditional Christian bestiaries and iconography developed additional lion symbolism not explicitly fixed by Scripture."

Nevertheless, Scripture uses lion imagery in materially opposite ways, including for Satan, violent enemies, empires, and divine judgment. The term therefore has a recognizable primary association but no single context-independent symbolic meaning."

BOOK ENTRY
A royal and devouring ruler or empire. Wicked rulers, Assyria, and Babylon bear the predatory figure; its rightful holder is the Lion of Judah.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Prov 28:15; Zeph 3:3; Jer 50:17; Ezek 19; Rev 5:5) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Proverbs 28:15 — As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.
Zephaniah 3:3 — Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves; they gnaw not the bones till the morrow.
Jeremiah 50:17 — Israel is a scattered sheep; the lions have driven him away: first the king of Assyria hath devoured him; and last this Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath broken his bones.
Ezekiel 19:1 — Moreover take thou up a lamentation for the princes of Israel,
Ezekiel 19:2 — And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions.
Ezekiel 19:3 — And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men.
Ezekiel 19:4 — The nations also heard of him; he was taken in their pit, and they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt.
Ezekiel 19:5 — Now when she saw that she had waited, and her hope was lost, then she took another of her whelps, and made him a young lion.
Ezekiel 19:6 — And he went up and down among the lions, he became a young lion, and learned to catch the prey, and devoured men.
Ezekiel 19:7 — And he knew their desolate palaces, and he laid waste their cities; and the land was desolate, and the fulness thereof, by the noise of his roaring.
Ezekiel 19:8 — Then the nations set against him on every side from the provinces, and spread their net over him: he was taken in their pit.
Ezekiel 19:9 — And they put him in ward in chains, and brought him to the king of Babylon: they brought him into holds, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel.
Ezekiel 19:10 — Thy mother is like a vine in thy blood, planted by the waters: she was fruitful and full of branches by reason of many waters.
Ezekiel 19:11 — And she had strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule, and her stature was exalted among the thick branches, and she appeared in her height with the multitude of her branches.
Ezekiel 19:12 — But she was plucked up in fury, she was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up her fruit: her strong rods were broken and withered; the fire consumed them.
Ezekiel 19:13 — And now she is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty ground.
Ezekiel 19:14 — And fire is gone out of a rod of her branches, which hath devoured her fruit, so that she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule. This is a lamentation, and shall be for a lamentation.
Revelation 5:5 — And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
